label: modern_population_sensitivity
label_text: Policy experiments on the modern population: not replays or costings of any past event.

diagnosis.evidence: pe-uk variables/gov/hmrc/income_tax/adjusted_net_income.py at 2.132.6 and 2.143.0. docs/uk_replay/evidence/policy_experiments/swap_mechanisms.py and README.md: a parent on £62,000 with £4,000 of employee pension contributions and one child has adjusted net income of £62,000 and a £135 charge on 2.132.6, £58,000 and no charge on 2.143.0.
diagnosis.fixed_in: policyengine-uk 2.134.8 (1dbc88172, 'fix: include relieved pension contributions in adjusted net income')
diagnosis.summary: ITA 2007 s. 58 deducts relieved pension contributions in adjusted net income, which sets the charge's taper. pe-uk 2.132.6 deducted only grossed-up Gift Aid, so savers' adjusted net income was too high and more of them paid the charge. 2.143.0 deducts the relief, and the charge raises £0.13bn to 0.15bn less.

diagnosis.fixed_in: policyengine-uk 2.134.8 (1dbc88172, 'fix: include relieved pension contributions in adjusted net income')
diagnosis.summary: ITA 2007 s. 58 deducts relieved pension contributions in adjusted net income, which sets the charge's taper. pe-uk 2.132.6 deducted only grossed-up Gift Aid, so savers' adjusted net income was too high and more of them paid the charge. 2.143.0 deducts the relief, and the charge raises £0.13bn to 0.15bn less.

Both sides of this change come from one model fix. 2.132.6 charges every home buyer's whole stock of other residential property at the higher rates (policyengine-uk#2238), and its scale lacks Autumn Budget 2024's further 2pp, so its £0.94bn is a 1pp removal on an overstated base. 2.143.0 has the full scale but takes the additional-dwelling purchase as a dataset input, which the interim cut does not supply, so it returns 0. Neither number is the surcharge's yield; the pre-Budget cut imputes the purchases (microcosm#1308).

diagnosis.evidence: pe-uk stamp_duty/residential/purchase/main/first/* at 2.132.6 and 2.143.0; the artifacts' modern_processed readback (first.max 500,000 against 625,000 in 2024)
diagnosis.fixed_in: policyengine-uk 2.141.8 (4044d6ccf, 'Fix recent residential SDLT purchase schedules and inclusive first-buyer caps')
diagnosis.summary: In 2024-25, 2.143.0 has the Growth Plan relief: first-time buyers pay nothing to £425,000 on prices to £625,000, against a main-scale nil band of £250,000. 2.132.6 has the 2017 limits (£300,000 and 500,000) against a £125,000 band. Zeroing the limit therefore removes a smaller relief on 2.143.0. In 2025-26 both engines have the same limits.

diagnosis.fixed_in: policyengine-uk 2.139.4 (83de1ef1d, 'Correct historical dividend income tax band thresholds')
diagnosis.summary: pe-uk 2.132.6 keeps the dividend additional-rate threshold at £150,000 until April 2026 (and the higher-rate threshold at £37,500), so its reversal misses the dividend band in 2024-25 and 2025-26; 2.143.0 has the statutory £125,140 and £37,700. The difference is the dividend band's yield.

diagnosis.fixed_in: policyengine-uk 2.141.8 (4044d6ccf, 'Fix recent residential SDLT purchase schedules and inclusive first-buyer caps')
diagnosis.summary: pe-uk 2.132.6 has no Growth Plan SDLT relief, so removing it moved nothing; 2.143.0 has the relief, and the experiment returns -£1.234bn against the OBR's -£1.048bn.

diagnosis.evidence: pe-uk parameters/gov/simulation/microdata_vat_coverage.yaml (0.38 at 2.132.6; 0.469 = 0.67 x 0.7 at 2.143.0) and utils/vat.py; policyengine-uk#1996 (98ab77093) and 691267f5c, both first in 2.135.7. The modern-law VAT aggregate falls by 0.810 in both years, which is 0.38 / 0.469.
diagnosis.summary: policyengine-uk 2.135.7 splits VAT grossing into the survey's consumption coverage and the household share of receipts (0.67 x 0.7 = 0.469, replacing the combined 0.38, with the derivation in docs/engineering/vat-coverage.md). VAT on recorded consumption is divided by that factor, so every VAT effect scales by 0.810. The rate rise's scaled ratio to the OBR moves from 1.31 to 1.06.

diagnosis.evidence: pe-uk variables/gov/hmrc/income_tax/bracketized_savings_income/savings_starter_rate_income.py at 2.132.6 and 2.143.0. docs/uk_replay/evidence/policy_experiments/swap_mechanisms.py and README.md: a person with £20,000 of earnings and £3,000 of interest in 2025 keeps the whole starting-rate band on 2.132.6 (removing the allowance changes nothing) and has none on 2.143.0 (removing it costs £200).
diagnosis.fixed_in: policyengine-uk 2.139.2 (35f992c6a, 'Correct the savings starting-rate taper', fixing #1799)
diagnosis.summary: pe-uk 2.132.6 started the starting-rate taper at the personal allowance plus the £5,000 band, applied to income already net of the allowance, so it kept the whole 0% band for anyone with taxable non-savings income up to £17,570; both versions' code comments read ITA 2007 s. 12 as removing it from the first pound. Those savers' interest sat in the 0% band, where the allowance does nothing. 2.143.0 tapers from the first pound, so more interest falls in the basic and higher bands, where the allowance relieves it: the reversal's scaled ratio moves from 0.43 to 0.73.
